Everything else in the book — its title page, its twenty TOPIC 1.x banners, and all 39 'Refer to the Grade 1 Learner's Book' cross-references — says Grade 1, so this is a leftover rather than an ambiguity. Both sentences named Cookery, Recreation, Energy and Designing, which this book does not teach, and Computer and Travel, which it teaches under other names — while omitting Tools and Equipment, Drama, ICT Devices in Everyday Life and Graphic Communication entirely. //subtextAddress: The imprint page names the publisher and its street in one breath — "Zambia Educational Publishing House Light Industrial Area" — because the manuscript typed them with a single space between. The engine turns a run of five or more spaces into a real line break (that is how a Word-typed address usually arrives) and a single space gives it nothing to go on, so the two have to be parted here. Every other ZEPH imprint page sets the publisher on its own line above the street.

One does the opposite, breaking a single sentence across two bullets ("Establish relationships, patterns and" / "make connections."), and is closed back up. //replaceBlocks: PROOFREADING ROUND 1, comments #937 + #943 (one instruction, not two: the reviewer pasted the same 52-entry glossary twice — once on the contents page asking for it to be listed there, once on the last content page asking for the pages themselves). The manuscript ships no glossary at all, so this grafts one in as back matter. The anchor is the first block of the BACK COVER; it is replaced by the glossary followed by a verbatim `raw` copy of itself, which is how an append is expressed with replaceBlocks. `h1` gives the section its own page and a contents entry; the cts theme sets tocUnitsOnly:false, so the TOC line #937 asks for lands automatically after TOPIC 1.20 and needs no separate override. Entries are plain 'Term: meaning' paragraphs because formatGlossary() runs after applyOverrides() and styles them itself (bold term + ': ' + meaning), so the house glossary look is not hand-built here. Text transcribed programmatically from the reviewer's own note in zeph.db, not retyped.

with.para: Analytical Thinking: The ability to examine information carefully, break problems into smaller parts and find possible solutions.
Assessment: The process of checking what learners know, understand and can do.
Collaboration: Working together with others to achieve a common goal.
Colouring: Filling a drawing or picture with colour to make it clear and attractive.
Communication: The process of sharing information, ideas, thoughts and feelings with others.
Computer: An electronic device used to process, store and display information.
Computer Software: Programmes that give instructions to a computer and help it perform different tasks.
Creativity: The ability to use imagination and ideas to create or do something new.
Critical Thinking: The ability to think carefully, ask questions, examine information and make simple decisions.
Digital Device: An electronic device that can receive, process, store or communicate information.
Digital Literacy: The ability to use digital devices safely, appropriately and effectively.
Drama: An activity in which people act out characters, situations or stories.
Emotional Intelligence: The ability to recognise and manage one's emotions and understand the feelings of others.
Entrepreneur: A person who starts and manages a business.
Entrepreneurship: The knowledge, skills and attitudes involved in starting and managing a business.
Environmental Sustainability: The responsible use and protection of the environment and natural resources.
Equipment: Items used to carry out a particular activity or task.
Financial Literacy: Knowledge and skills needed to earn, save, spend and manage money responsibly.
Fitness: The ability of the body to perform physical activities effectively and remain healthy.
Freehand Drawing: Drawing without using a ruler or another instrument to guide the lines.
Hand Tool: A simple tool operated by hand to perform a particular task.
Hardware: The physical parts of a computer or digital device that can be seen and touched.
Health: A state of physical, mental and social well-being.
Hospitality: The act of welcoming, helping and caring for guests or visitors.
ICT: Information and Communication Technology; the use of technology to create, process, store and communicate information.
ICT Device: An electronic device used to create, process, store or communicate information.
Innovation: The introduction or use of a new idea, method or way of doing something.
Internet: A worldwide network that connects computers and other digital devices for communication and sharing information.
Lettering: The art of writing or designing letters in a clear and attractive way.
Materials: Substances or items used to make or create something.
Modelling: The process of making a three-dimensional object by shaping materials such as clay or plasticine.
Needlework: The making or decorating of items using a needle, thread and fabric.
Online Safety: Safe and responsible behaviour when using the internet and digital devices.
Pattern: A repeated arrangement of lines, shapes, colours, sounds or objects.
Posture: The way a person holds or positions the body when sitting, standing, walking or performing an activity.
Problem Solving: The process of finding ways to deal with a problem or challenge.
Protective Clothing: Clothing worn to protect the body from injury, dirt or other dangers.
Recycling: The process of using materials again instead of throwing them away.
Role-Play: Acting out a situation, character or role to help learners understand an idea or situation.
Safety: Being protected from danger, injury or harm.
Sketching: Making a simple drawing using lines and shapes.
Software: Programmes or instructions that tell a computer or digital device what to do.
Sound: Something that can be heard by the ears.
Specialised Room: A room designed or equipped for a particular activity or purpose.
Sports Skills: Abilities used when taking part in sports and games.
Structure: Something that is built or formed and has a particular shape or purpose.
Swimming: The activity of moving through water using the body.
Tourism: The activity of travelling to places for enjoyment, learning or other purposes.
Tourist: A person who travels to another place for a visit.
Utensil: A tool or object used for a particular task, especially in cooking.
Visual Information: Information that is communicated through pictures, signs, symbols, diagrams or objects.
Waste: Materials or things that are no longer wanted or needed.

//editAllExercise1: PROOFREADING ROUND 1, comment #939. The reviewer pasted an exercise to be inserted under LEARNING ACTIVITY 1, but the text they pasted is the storage-place exercise that is ALREADY EXERCISE 1 under LEARNING ACTIVITY 2 on the facing page — and they separately renumbered that existing box to EXERCISE 2 rather than deleting it, so applying the paste literally would have printed two near-identical storage exercises back to back, the first under a cleaning activity it has nothing to do with. Read instead as what actually differs between their version and the book's: the real answers. The manuscript's box only carries the rubric 'Learner correctly matches each item with its appropriate storage place', which tells a teacher nothing; the reviewer supplies the five matches. So the existing box is upgraded in place, under the activity it belongs to, and no exercise is added or renumbered. Decided with the user, who chose this reading over applying the paste verbatim. The reviewer's 'Expected Answer:'/'Expected Performance:' labels are deliberately NOT carried over - house style renders an expected answer as plain italic with no label, which the engine already does by stripping them.
//editAllActivityNumbers: QA PASS (not a reviewer comment). The book numbers its LEARNING ACTIVITY headings two different ways. In five of the eight topics that have more than one sub-topic (1.2, 1.8, 1.11, 1.13, 1.16) the activities run CONTINUOUSLY through the topic, so Topic 1.13 reads 1..6 straight across its two sub-topics. In two (1.3, 1.4) they restart at 1 in each sub-topic, so Topic 1.3 prints two separate 'LEARNING ACTIVITY 1' headings. Exercises, by contrast, run continuously in EVERY topic including these two - Topic 1.3's run 1..6 - so the restart is not a deliberate per-sub-topic scheme, just an inconsistency. House style is that the same element may not look different on different pages, so the two outliers are brought over to the majority's continuous numbering. Done as five surgical renames rather than with `renumberActivities`, for two reasons: that key resets its counter only at 'UNIT N' and 'LESSON N' banners, neither of which this primary family uses (it uses TOPIC/SUB-TOPIC), so it would number all 61 activities 1..61 across the whole book; and it would also silently renumber Topic 1.1, whose sequence is broken by a duplicated heading in the manuscript that is still with the reviewer - masking that defect instead of leaving it visible. Each `find` carries its activity's full title, and every one of those titles is unique in the book.
//editAllHeadingCase: QA PASS (not a reviewer comment). Four LEARNING ACTIVITY titles print out of step with the other 57, which are all Title Case. Two shout a single word mid-title (ACTIVITIES, ITEMS); the engine preserves an all-caps word inside an otherwise mixed heading in case it is an acronym, which is what correctly protects ICT elsewhere in this book, but neither of these is one. The manuscript is messier than that - six of its titles shout in full caps - but the engine's uniformBoxTitleCase pass already brings those over on the way out, so only these two survive into the PDF. `headingCase` was tried first and backed out: it is the documented key for settling a book's heading case, but on this book it fixed eight titles and broke nine, because TITLE_SMALL (which it uses) lists 'using' while the engine's own unasked pass explicitly refuses to lower it - 'never Using, a participle that title case capitalises' - so seven correct headings lost their capital, and its recase regex treats a hyphenated compound as a single word, flattening 'Role-Playing' to 'Role-playing' and 'Free-Form' to 'Free-form'. Two surgical renames are the smaller, safer change. NOTE the direction of the second one: this book capitalises Using everywhere else ('Making Products Using Hand Tools', 'Locating Landmarks Using Cardinal Points'), and this title only lost its capital because it arrived in full caps and was rebuilt through TITLE_SMALL - so it gains the capital back rather than its siblings losing theirs.
//topic11PlaygroundActivity: QA PASS (not a reviewer comment). TOPIC 1.1 printed two LEARNING ACTIVITY 3 headings, so its activities ran 1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5. The second box is not a duplicate activity: it is the PLAYGROUND activity, pasted in under a second copy of the specialised-rooms heading together with that activity’s entire sixteen-line prologue. The importer shows it exactly — the second activity block opens with body items byte-identical to the first block’s complete body (Learner’s Book ref, materials, and all nine procedure steps), and only then begins its own material: playground equipment, its own eight-step procedure, its own Teacher’s Brief Notes, LET’S TALK AND LEARN, LET’S DO and EXERCISE 2. The manuscript settles what it is without anyone having to guess. Learner’s Book references run Page 4 for specialised rooms, pages 5–6 for this block (stated in its own Brief Notes), Pages 7–8 for the road and Pages 9–10 for posture — a continuous ascending sequence in which the playground is unambiguously the FOURTH activity of the topic, between specialised rooms and road safety. So the duplicated prologue is deleted, the block is renumbered 4, and the road and posture activities move to 5 and 6. INFERRED, and the one thing here not read off the manuscript: the wording of the new title. The block carries no title of its own, so it takes the parallel form of its sibling — “Practising Safety Rules in Specialised Rooms” becomes “Practising Safety Rules on the Playground”. If the author worded it differently in the syllabus, that line is the one to change. NOT fixed here, and still the reviewer’s: the topic’s EXERCISE numbering, which runs 1, 2, 3, 5. Every other topic in the book gives each activity exactly one exercise; this one now has six activities and four exercises, so exercises are genuinely missing rather than merely mis-numbered, and comments #940-942 cannot be applied until the author supplies them.
